rust.note: Both programs have a quiet main entry and print one line. Grail uses a builtin function call; Rust println! is a formatting macro. Grail uses checked call-scoped borrowing so owners remain usable after println.
Grail uses var for reassignment; Rust uses let mut. Both distinguish a fixed binding from a reassignable one.

Grail num arithmetic always wraps and comparisons yield numbers. Rust has bool, many numeric types, and explicit wrapping operations. Ordinary Rust overflow panics when overflow checks are enabled (normally debug builds) and wraps when disabled.
Both support native recursion. Rust can return a trailing expression; Grail uses return for non-unit results and allows implicit unit returns. This example makes no performance claim.
Grail let fixes the binding but allows checked mutation of the owned object. Rust requires mut for Vec mutation. Grail’s bytes is specialized; Rust uses the general Vec<u8> type.
Both lengths count UTF-8 bytes. Grail string literals here are owned strings; Rust string literals are borrowed static str values, so this comparison explicitly constructs a String.

Both ranges are half-open and bounds-checked. Rust slices are borrowed pointer/length values. The current Grail runtime allocates view descriptors; do not infer zero-allocation views from this syntax.
Both transfer owned buffers by move and clean up the callee-owned value. Grail’s affine ownership is not presented as something Rust lacks.
Both reject using an owner after a move. Repair either version by using the new owner, borrowing, or explicitly cloning/copying data.
Both can end a borrow at last use. Rust calls this non-lexical lifetimes; this is a shared capability, not a Grail-only feature.
Both reject vector growth while a reader is still live. Reallocation would invalidate that reader.
Rust spells the readonly reborrow as &*writer. Grail spells it read(writer). Both suspend conflicting exclusive access until the readonly child’s last use.
Grail exchange and load make storage operations explicit. Rust uses a standard-library replace function and dereference syntax; both return the old value without losing its ownership.

Grail names lifetime parameters without apostrophes. Rust could elide this single input/output lifetime; it is written explicitly here to show the relationship. Rust shared references are Copy; Grail view handles passed by value are affine and may require explicit derivation.
Both reject returning a view into a local owner. A lifetime annotation cannot keep that allocation alive.
Both support partial moves and drop the remaining owned fields. Rust’s String construction makes the owned-text comparison explicit.
Grail vec_pop aborts on an empty vector. Rust Vec::pop returns Option, letting ordinary code handle emptiness instead of unwrapping it. Both protect element references from reallocation.
Both match tagged variants and move owned payloads into an arm. Rust patterns qualify variants; Grail’s consuming match uses the unqualified variant names in these examples.

Rust supplies Result in its library; Grail declares the enum here. Both support ? propagation. Grail ! aborts without unwinding; Rust unwrap panics, with unwinding or abort determined by panic configuration.

Grail marks declarations with type T and uses explicit constructor arguments here. Rust has broader contextual inference and a standard Option. Both instantiate generic layouts and type-directed cleanup.
Grail writes identity<num>; Rust uses a turbofish, identity::<u64>. Both infer the buffer instantiation and specialize generic code.
Both reject this unconstrained generic body even when called with a copyable integer. Rust can opt into T: Copy or Clone bounds; Grail does not yet offer that trait mechanism.

Both must preserve the lifetime of the newly stored borrow. Rust elides the slot lifetime here. Grail’s current weak-update checker may retain old guards longer, and rejects some opaque external writes that Rust can express.

Both use deterministic scope-based destruction on normal exits, including continue and early return. Rust supports custom Drop implementations; the Grail examples rely on generated default cleanup. Neither example establishes comparative performance.
